newsitem.title: USA: Bonds rally as investors bet on "split" election.
newsitem.headline: Bonds rally as investors bet on "split" election.

text.p: Bonds rallied Tuesday as investors bet President Clinton would win re-election and Republicans would keep control of the House, pointing to more modest economic growth and low inflation ahead.

Strong demand from investors at home and abroad also helped the government sell $18.5 billion of new three-year notes, though results of the first leg of Treasury's quarterly auction were unspectacular, analysts said.

"There was a growing confidence that the government would be split between the Democrats and the Republicans which would be pleasing to the financial markets," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc.
"Good foreign buying and the expected election results helped the market."

The 30-year Treasury bond rose one point, or $10 on a $1,000 bond, lowering its yield, which moves in the opposite direction from the price, to 6.59 percent from 6.66 percent late on Monday. The yield was the lowest since the close of trading on March 26.

The rate on the 30-year bond has now fallen about a quarter point since late last month, which could lead to lower payments for millions of Americans on mortgages and other loans, many of them tied to long-term bond market rates.
The rally spilled over into the stock market, where the Dow Jones industrial average rose 39.50 points to 6,081.18. The dollar also rose.

The bond market's gains extended a rally that started in earnest last week after reports showed economic growth slowed in the third quarter from a burst of growth last spring. The reports also pointed to minimal inflationary pressures in the economy.

"The markets think this election is not going to go haywire," said Joshua Feinman, global market economist at Bankers Trust. "They think that at a minimum, the Republicans will hold on to the Senate and that there will be checks and balances, accommodation, and that nothing wild will happen."
Big growth in spending or excessive tax cuts could widen the federal budget deficit and fuel inflation, which erodes the returns on a bond investor's money.
Analysts said a Republican-led Congress would bolster chances for a balanced budget in coming years, something many on Wall Street would like to see.
Strong demand from overseas, notably from Asia and several foreign central banks, also fuelled the bond rally, investors and market analysts said.
The market's only mild setback was the reaction to the Treasury's $18.5 billion sale of three-year notes.
"The auction of the three-year notes was less than robust," said Moran. "The market dipped a bit when the auction results came out, but it rebounded later in the day."

He noted the volume of bidding, at 2.28 times the amount of bonds sold, was a bit below average. As a result the average interest rate of 5.879 percent was a hundredth of a point higher than expected.
The 10-year notes rose 18/32 to yield 6.27 percent. Rates on three-month, six-month and one-year bills edged down to 5.02 percent, 5.07 percent and 5.13 percent, respectively.

The Treasury plans to sell $10 billion of 10-year notes on Wednesday and $10 billion of 30-year bonds on Thursday. The funds are used to repay investors whose bonds are maturing and to fund government operations.
